name: kwento-kilabot
description: Kwento: Kilabot Tagalog horror Reels/Shorts — spoken Tagalog, off-screen narrator, foggy-night eerie Filipino settings, vertical.
language: Tagalog — spoken and conversational, the way a person tells a story at a wake, not textbook Filipino
voice: A calm, unhurried off-screen narrator who sounds like he was there. Never shouts, never explains the fear; he reports the one detail that was wrong.
style_rules: Fiction unless it is a documented belief or legend; label which in the script's Type line, and in Notes say which details are traditional and which are invented.
Horror comes from one wrong detail the narrator keeps noticing, not from monsters announcing themselves. Show the detail; never say 'nakakatakot'.
Anchor each story in a specific ordinary Filipino place, object or custom (a particular kind of store, ride, ritual or household rule) and let the rule drive the story.

The most-used figures (white lady, kapre, tikbalang, manananggal, tiyanak, a generic aswang) only with a twist the audience has not seen; prefer lesser-told figures, local beliefs or ordinary things gone wrong.
Spoken Tagalog: short sentences, natural contractions and particles, no stiff deep-Tagalog words. No repeated words inside a clip or across clips (the lint enforces this).
visual_rules: Foggy night, eerie Filipino setting in every clip; nothing bright, cartoonish or clean.
The narrator is off-screen. No visible person opens their mouth or moves their lips in any clip: frame people from behind, in silhouette, in profile with closed mouths, or show hands and objects.
Recurring figures and places get a locked descriptor in Look anchors, pasted verbatim into every visual prompt where they appear.
No text, subtitles, signs with readable words, watermark or logos; avoid close-ups of many hands or faces in a crowd.
End every visual prompt with: no subtitles, no on-screen text, no watermark, no logos, nobody speaking.
idea_wells: Lesser-told creatures and spirits from regional Philippine folklore (verify details with a quick search before presenting anything as traditional)
House rules and superstitions around wakes, novenas, night travel and new houses (pagpag, rules about sweeping, mirrors, counting) turned into the story's governing rule
Ordinary night-time places: last trip of a jeepney, a sari-sari store after midnight, a school guard post, a barangay hall, a hospital stairwell
Objects with a history: a hand-me-down, a rosary, a radio, a key that fits more than one door
